overview:
Guyana is the only country in South America where English is the official language. It sits on the continent's northeastern shoulder, facing the Atlantic Ocean, with Venezuela to the west, Brazil to the south and Suriname to the east. At about 215,000 km² it is roughly the size of the US state of Idaho, but only about 800,000 people live there, nearly all of them on a narrow coastal strip that lies below sea level and is protected by a long seawall.

The capital, Georgetown, is a city of wooden colonial buildings and canals, home to St. George's Cathedral, one of the tallest wooden churches in the world. Inland, the country is almost entirely rainforest, rivers and savanna, with few roads. The name Guyana comes from an Indigenous word meaning "land of many waters."

Guyanese people trace their roots to India, Africa, Indigenous nations, Europe and China. Guyana is a republic with an elected president. Sugar, rice, gold and bauxite were long its main products; huge oil discoveries offshore since 2015 have made it one of the fastest-growing economies on Earth.
landAndNature:
About 80 percent of Guyana is covered by rainforest, part of the vast Guiana Shield, one of the largest untouched wildernesses left in the tropics. Great rivers such as the Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice flow north to the coast, broken by rapids and falls. Kaieteur Falls on the Potaro River drops about 226 meters in a single plunge, roughly four times the height of Niagara, and a tiny golden frog lives its whole life inside the giant bromeliad plants around it.

In the southwest, the Rupununi savanna spreads out beneath the Kanuku Mountains. Guyana is home to giants: the jaguar, the giant anteater, the giant river otter, the harpy eagle, the arapaima, one of the largest freshwater fish, the black caiman, and the Victoria amazonica water lily, whose leaves can be two meters across.
peopleAndCulture:
Descendants of Indian indentured workers make up the largest group, followed by Afro-Guyanese, people of mixed heritage and nine Indigenous nations such as the Makushi and Wapishana. English is official, but most people speak Guyanese Creole day to day, and Hindu, Christian and Muslim holidays are all national celebrations: Diwali lamps, Christmas masquerades and Eid feasts.

The food reflects this mix. Pepperpot, a dark stew flavored with cassareep made from cassava, is an Indigenous dish eaten at Christmas; curry and roti, cook-up rice and Chinese-style fried rice are everyday favorites. Cricket is the national sport, and Guyana hosts matches for the West Indies team. Mashramani, on Republic Day in February, brings costume parades, calypso and steel bands to the streets of Georgetown.
history:
Arawak, Carib, Warao and other peoples lived along Guyana's rivers for thousands of years. Dutch traders settled in the early 1600s and built dikes and canals to farm the coast, bringing enslaved Africans to work sugar plantations. In 1763 an enslaved man named Cuffy led a major uprising in Berbice; he is now a national hero. Britain took over in 1814 and named the colony British Guiana.

After slavery ended in 1834, planters brought about 240,000 indentured workers from India between 1838 and 1917. Guyana became independent on May 26, 1966, and a republic in 1970. Politics has often divided along ethnic lines. Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, about two-thirds of Guyana's territory, a dispute now before the International Court of Justice. Since oil began flowing in 2019, the country has been changing rapidly.
funFacts: Kaieteur Falls is about 226 meters high, roughly four times the height of Niagara Falls, and sits deep in the rainforest.
Most of Guyana's coast lies below sea level, protected by a seawall first built by Dutch engineers.
The Victoria amazonica water lily, Guyana's national flower, has floating leaves strong enough to hold a small child.
Guyana is the only country in South America with English as its official language.
Guyana's national dish, pepperpot, is preserved by cassareep, a cassava sauce that keeps the stew edible for days without refrigeration.
Ninety percent of Guyanese live on a coastal strip that makes up only about 10 percent of the country.
